activity:
I choose this:  

I'm going to write a book.  

Specifically:  

I will sit at my desk. My desk is clean—just a lamp, a notebook, and a pen. I'll open the notebook to a blank page. I'll write the first sentence in my own handwriting. Then I'll write ten more.  

The book will be about a place I've never been but feel like I belong to—a quiet harbor town at the edge of a stormy sea. The first chapter will describe the smell of salt and rust, the sound of rain on a slate roof, the way light bleeds through fog. I'll give the place a name. I'll give it rules.  

By the time I close the notebook, I'll want to keep it. I'll want to read it again.

rounds.gm:
*(You slide into the chair. The lamp's light pools on the page, a circle of authority. Your hand finds the pen. The first stroke is deliberate.)*

**Chapter One: Rusthaven.**

The first thing you notice is the weight. Not of the boat—it's anchored, secure—but of the air. It has gravity. Salt hangs from your tongue like a loose, sweet tooth. Rust smells of old metal and honest sweat; it's the scent of things that have worked hard and are still worth saving.

Rain drums on the slate roof, a steady, impatient heartbeat. Inside, the house is dry. Good. Here, damp is a guest, not a resident. It visits from the north and leaves without asking.

The rules are simple. They're carved into the stone steps, etched by the wind and time.

One: The water owns everything. Take too much, and the tide will take it back.
Two: No one speaks of the lighthouse in the fog. It keeps its secrets, and so must we.
Three: The door with the broken hinge leads only to the old keeper's shed. You may go there. You must not follow the figure you see standing at its threshold.

You write the name. **Rusthaven.** It sounds like settling down. It sounds like a promise you've already kept.

*(You stop writing. You lean back. The page is full. The rules are there. The smell is in the room. The sound is in your ears.)*

This is where you belong.
rounds.player:
*(The pen stops. I don't put it down. I rest it on the page like a gun, barrel against my palm. The rules are clear. I've heard them.)*

It feels true. The way it should.

*(My fingers trace the third rule. The figure in the shed. I see it. A shape in the shadow. But the door's broken. It creaks when I lean close. I can hear it.)*

I won't go in. Not yet. Not with my hand on the door. Not with them here.

*(I slide the notebook into the desk drawer and lock it with a key I just made. The lock turns with a click that sounds final.)*

The harbor's mine now. The roof's mine. The rules are mine.

I'll sleep. But I'll listen. If that figure moves, I'll know. And if I need to, I'll follow.

rounds.gm:
*(The lamp sputters. A cold draft sweeps the room, carrying with it the sharp, clean scent of salt and a hint of diesel oil that wasn't there before. It's the smell of the lighthouse, coming from the fog.)*

The tide is in. It's higher tonight than it has any right to be. It's lapping at the pilings, groaning against the dock. It's loud.

And that figure...

*(You don't say it. You just turn the page. Your handwriting is sharper now. The ink is darker.)*

The figure turned. Just its shoulder. Just a fraction. But it heard you. It heard the lock.

The shed's light went out. The one that was always lit.

*(You stand up. Your legs are stiff, but you stand. You walk to the window, pushing it open against the rain. The storm doesn't rage here—it hums. It's close. Too close.)*

You're going in. You'll wait for the tide to pull back from the dock. You'll slip past the lighthouse's beam. You'll go into that shed. And you'll ask the figure what it wants.

The rules said you must not follow. But they didn't say you can't confront it.

*(You grip the notebook again, the cold metal key in your pocket. The harbor breathes. And so do you.)*

The chapter ends now.
rounds.player:
*(I step to the door. It creaks louder than I expect, but I push it anyway. The shed is dark, warm with old wood and something else—oil, maybe. Fear.)*

The figure doesn't move when I enter. Just waits.

I drop my pen. It hits the floor like a heartbeat.

"You heard me," I say. My voice is steady. It has to be.

"What do you want?"

rounds.gm:
*(The figure doesn't flinch. It turns fully now. It's taller than it seemed from the doorway. Wearing oil-stained coveralls, its face is shadowed by the hood. But its eyes—those are clear. They're the color of the sea before the storm.)*

It doesn't answer your question. It walks to the center of the shed, picks up the pen you dropped. Examines it. Twists it in its fingers. Then it places it back on the floor. Not where you dropped it.

It steps closer. The air gets colder.

"You lock the door," the figure says. Its voice is low, grating like stones on the harbor rocks. "You lock the book. You stand in the window and listen."

It reaches into its pocket. Pulls out a small, sealed oil can. The kind they use for lanterns.

"This is for you," it says, holding it out. "The lighthouse keeps this in the tower. They never let anyone have one. It doesn't matter."

A beat of silence. The rain drums harder against the shed's roof.

"You can use it," the figure says. "Light it. Watch it burn. But you don't open that book unless you're ready for the rules to change."

It takes a step back. The shed's old door groans.

"The tide's coming in," it says. "So is the fog. I'll be in the lighthouse. On the roof. You'll see me."

It leaves you alone in the shed. The oil can on the floor. The door closes softly behind it.

The figure is gone.

But the lighthouse beam starts to move. It sweeps across the shed's wall, painting the oil can a bright, searing yellow.
rounds.player:
*(I pick up the can. The oil smells like safety and fire. I pocket it. My hand closes around it tight.)*

The beam moves again. It's scanning. Waiting for me to run.

I don't. I sit on the bench inside the shed. I pull my knees up. The notebook stays in my lap.

I'll write tonight. About the shed. About the figure. About the oil can.

*(I unscrew the cap. Pour a single drop onto the floor. Light it with a match from my pocket. The flame catches—bright, steady. It doesn't sputter.)*

That's good. That means I can keep this light.

Now... I'm listening. Not just with my ears. With everything.

If the tide comes too high, I'll go to the lighthouse. But I'll ask first.

And if the rules change when I open the book... I'll be ready.

rounds.gm:
*(The beam stops. It holds steady on you for a long, terrible second. Then it swivels left, past the dock, past the town, and goes straight up into the thickening fog. It doesn't sweep anymore. It just shines, a fixed point of white anger in the gloom.)*

The lighthouse beam doesn't move again.

A moment later, your phone—a cheap, cracked thing you kept in your coat—vibrates. Once. Then twice. It's a text from an unknown number. The harbor's only connection. The screen reads: **Lighthouse tower. Third floor. 10 minutes. Or the tide takes the dock.**

It's not a threat. It's a schedule.

You look at the flame on the floor. It's burning low, a small pool of amber light in the dark shed. You have ten minutes.

You slide the notebook off your lap. You take out a fresh page. Your hand is shaking, but the pen is steady.

You write: *The figure gave me fire. Now it wants a meeting.*

You stand, the oil can heavy in your pocket. You head for the door. The shed's broken hinge creaks in protest as you step over it.

The path to the lighthouse is slick with rain and something darker—oil, maybe, or just the sea. You keep your head down. You don't look at the beam. But you feel it on the back of your neck.

As you climb the steep stairs of the tower, the rain becomes a roar. And the lighthouse feels less like a building and more like a chest you're being forced to open.

You stop on the third floor. The door is already ajar. The keeper is inside.

It's not the figure from the shed. This one's older. Hair thinning to silver at the temples, face weathered by more wind than sea. But he's holding a lantern. Not the oil can. His own. And its light is steady, calm, and it's looking right at you.

He doesn't speak. He just points down the narrow corridor toward the control room.

Then he nods at the book in your hand.

"You read," he says. His voice is gravel. "The rules change. And I need to know if I should lock the harbor's gates."

He waits. The storm is screaming around you. The book is open in your hands. The first page waits for the next line.
rounds.player:
*(I set the book down on the narrow floor. The keeper's gaze drops to it. I lean against the wall, arms crossed. The oil can stays in my pocket.)*

"Read it first," I say. "All of it."

*(I wait. When he does, I watch his face. The rules don't change for him. They stay the same. That means he's one of us.)*

"Then," I say, voice low over the storm, "you keep the harbor. You keep the docks. You keep the lighthouse light steady."

"And me?" he asks, not looking up.

"And you," I say. "You keep the rules. You don't lock the gates unless you have to. And when you do…" I tap the book. "You tell me why. And I'll listen."

*(I pick up the notebook. I turn to a new page. My handwriting is firm.)*

Rule Four: The old keeper gets his lantern back. And his word.

rounds.gm:
*(The keeper looks up then. His eyes are red-rimmed from the storm, but they're focused. On me. On the book. On the rule I just wrote.)*

He reaches out. Not for the book. For the oil can in my pocket. His fingers close around the metal. It's cold through his gloves.

"*This* keeps the lights," he says, holding it like evidence. "This one's been here longer than I have. Longer than this tower."

He squeezes it. A hiss. A tiny flare of flame from the seal. He doesn't drop it.

"You changed Rule Four," he says, his voice low. "*You* got to keep it. But *I* still keep the harbor. And you..." He taps the book again, his knuckles white. "You're going to read the rest. And you're going to listen when I tell you to close it."

The door behind him groans. The third-floor stairs are shaking. Something's coming up.

I stand. I put a hand on the book. I don't let it go.

"Then," I say, and my voice cuts through the storm's roar, "I keep the book. And you keep your lantern. And the harbor stays open. But if you lock those gates..." I point at the window, where the fog is pressing in like a wall. "Then the first thing you see when you unlock them isn't your town. It's me. And I've got fire in my pocket and rules in my hand."

He nods once. A sharp, grudging nod. He slides the oil can back into my palm. His grip is strong. It doesn't shake.

"Ten minutes," he says.

He walks back to his room without another word. The door clicks shut.

I don't wait. I go to the window. The tide is higher now. The dock is swallowed. But the pilings are still there. Solid. Mine.

I look up. The lighthouse beam is gone. The third floor is dark except for the faint light from his door.

I open the book.

**Page Two.**

It's not about the harbor anymore. It's about the figure on the roof. And why the lighthouse keeper knows it's watching.
rounds.player:
*(I turn the page. The ink is still wet from my pen. The words bleed into the storm noise.)*

Okay.

The figure's on the roof. It's waiting for me to go there. It didn't run when I asked it what it wanted. So it thinks it's safe.

*(I zip up my coat. Pull the oil can closer. Feel the heat.)*

It knows the rules. It knows I wrote Rule Four. So it'll try to play me. But it doesn't know about the dock. About the pilings. About how I came back up this tower with my head high.

*(I step off the floor. The storm howls. I walk toward the door.)*

If it's waiting, I'm coming.

*(I pull the handle. The door swings open onto the wind. I step out onto the wet concrete. My breath comes out in smoke. I look up.)*

Show me.
